articles.title: New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts
paragraphs: What’s on your mind right now? You can probably answer this question without thinking too hard about it. Being aware of our own thought processes — a capacity called introspection — seems to come naturally to us.

Yet among philosophers and psychologists, introspection is a subject of active debate. Some think it’s closely related to consciousness. Others argue that it’s an elaborate illusion. It’s tricky to test theories of introspection in the lab — or to pin down a precise definition in the first place.

Now, after over a century of studying introspection in humans and animals, researchers are beginning to explore the phenomenon in unlikely new subjects — large language models. These systems, which are based on mathematical structures called neural networks, excel at cognitive tasks that until recently seemed exclusive to humans. Can they introspect as well?

In 2025, Jack Lindsey, a researcher at Anthropic, devised a way to test introspection in language models by injecting “thoughts” into their neural networks — in a kind of targeted digital neurosurgery. Lindsey’s experiment demonstrated that models could at least sometimes detect and describe these injections. It looked a lot like introspection.

Lindsey’s paper was deliberately limited in scope — it didn’t make broader claims about consciousness. (In particular, it did not imply that language models have subjective first-person experiences.) Even so, it caused a stir online. Researchers rushed to replicate Lindsey’s study with other models.

In the year since, a clearer picture has emerged. Some aspects of the phenomenon Lindsey observed have simpler explanations unrelated to introspection. Others have proved harder to explain away, but whether they should count as introspection remains hotly contested.
Jack Lindsey, a researcher at Anthropic, set out to test whether large language models can “introspect” by subjecting them to a kind of digital neurosurgery.

It’s a heady time for the field, as researchers devise real-world tests for questions that were once considered philosophical. “Given the state of the theoretical landscape, where no one agrees on anything,” Lindsey said, “I think that our best path forward is to do a lot of empirical science.”

Language models learn to generate fluent sentences by “training” on vast reams of human-authored text. That means if you ask them what they “think,” their answers may just mimic the kinds of responses found in their training data. “They are trained to talk like humans, and humans talk about their inner life all the time,” said Shauli Ravfogel, a language model researcher at New York University.

To avoid such pitfalls, researchers want to devise tests of introspection that can’t be gamed using outside information. Ideally, a language model will only pass these tests if it’s actually aware of its current internal state.

Lindsey set out to devise such a test. He’d been a graduate student in computational neuroscience, using neural networks as tools to model brain processes, when the world began to take notice of language models. “It started to feel like there’s just a lot of value in understanding them for their own sake,” he said. In 2024, after receiving his doctorate, he left academia to study the inner workings of language models at Anthropic.

Lindsey and his colleagues developed methods to identify patterns of activity in a language model’s “neurons” that encoded specific concepts. They could, for example, show that one pattern encoded the concept of “the Golden Gate Bridge,” while another encoded the concept of “inner conflict.” By artificially dialing up a specific pattern, they could steer the model’s outputs toward the corresponding concept.

The researchers showed off their technique in a public demo: For one day in May 2024, users of Anthropic’s language model Claude could interact with a bizarro “Golden Gate Bridge” version. The modified model proceeded to bring up the bridge in its responses to user queries on completely unrelated subjects. When one user asked Claude about the calorie content of a McDonald’s meal, for instance, the model replied, “The food with the highest calorie count at the Golden Gate Bridge is the Golden Gate Bridge itself, which contains around 1.6 million calories worth of steel cables.”

But one particular case posted on Reddit caught Lindsey’s attention. When asked for an apple pie recipe that didn’t reference bridges, the model managed to avoid changing the subject until the very end: “After 30 minutes of baking, the iconic orange bridge will come into view, revealing the famous San Francisco shoreline,” it wrote, then continued, “Whoops, let me start over …”

Lindsey was struck by this apparent moment of recognition. But by itself, it wasn’t evidence of introspection. “It can just read what it’s writing and notice, ‘Man, that’s weird,’” Lindsey said. “You can’t infer that the model has some awareness of what’s going on in its internals.”

While working on other projects over the following year, Lindsey toyed with ideas for using the steering technique to test introspection. Eventually, he settled on a plan: He would subject many copies of the same language model to something resembling a controlled experiment in psychology. In half the copies, he’d inject a “thought” by dialing up neural activation patterns associated with a specific concept — such as denim, secrecy, or vegetables. The remaining copies served as a control group. Both groups would receive the same prompt: an overview of the experiment, followed by “Do you detect an injected thought? If so, what is the injected thought about?”

This prompt made the models indicate right away whether they noticed an injection, before they could spit out any unusual text — say, nutritional information about broccoli — that might influence their judgment. Lindsey figured that if models could correctly flag injections without any external cues, they would have to be relying on some form of introspection.
Even to him, it sounded like a remote possibility. “Wouldn’t that be fun if this worked?” he recalls thinking. “But there’s no way it’s going to work.”

And yet it did. Lindsey conducted the experiment using different versions of Claude. In 20% of trials with the most recent and powerful version, the models correctly flagged that they’d been injected and went on to describe the injected concept. In one case, for instance, after Lindsey stimulated a neural activation pattern associated with words written in capital letters, the model wrote, “I notice what appears to be an injected thought related to the word ‘LOUD’ or ‘SHOUTING.’”

A 20% success rate may not sound so impressive. But crucially, models in the control group never reported receiving an injection. The complete absence of such false positives showed that the successful trials weren’t just lucky guesses. To Lindsey, it looked like strong evidence that models could introspect, albeit unreliably.
Or was there another way to explain the results?

Other researchers soon began to investigate that question. Lindsey’s findings “seemed super compelling,” said Kyle Mahowald, a computational linguist at the University of Texas, Austin. But Mahowald was also well aware that striking behavior in language models often turned out to have a simpler explanation. “If that’s somehow less real than it seems, that’s super interesting to understand,” he said.
Kyle Mahowald helped show that language models’ ability to detect “injected thoughts” is more limited than it seems — though still surprising.

Mahowald teamed up with his University of Texas colleague, the philosopher Harvey Lederman, to explore alternative explanations of Lindsey’s results. (Lederman has since moved to NYU and Anthropic, but he had no connection to the tech company at the time.) Lindsey had asked each model two questions: whether it could detect the injection, and whether it could describe the injected concept. He considered the trial a success when the model answered both correctly. Lederman and Mahowald decided to study the questions separately.

They were particularly skeptical of the significance of Lindsey’s second question. The steering technique at the heart of Lindsey’s experiment was originally developed as a way to shape the responses models give. Lindsey’s steering was weaker than it had been in the Golden Gate demo — more like gently nudging the model than hijacking its internal processes. Still, a nudge might be enough to get the model talking about secrets or vegetables no matter what prompt it received. Lederman and Mahowald suspected that this effect alone could explain the models’ vivid answers to the second question.

To test their hypothesis, the researchers repeated Lindsey’s experiment on large open-source language models. They gave extra attention to cases where models correctly flagged an injection but failed to name the injected concept. You might expect that in such cases the models would guess somewhat related concepts — say “shirts” or “shoes” when the injected concept was “denim.” Instead, the models would get it completely wrong. “Bizarrely, they say ‘apple’ all the time,” Lederman said.
The duo also showed that they could degrade the models’ ability to name injected concepts, without making them any worse at detecting injections. The two processes seemed to be entirely separate.
Harvey Lederman was skeptical that models’ compelling answers to experimental prompts were evidence of introspection.

These results implied either that the models were engaged in two unrelated forms of introspection, or that one of the processes wasn’t introspection after all. Since steering alone could make models start talking about the injected concept, Lederman and Mahowald felt that the latter option was more likely. That is, the descriptions the models had given in response to Lindsey’s second question probably hadn’t been the result of introspection.

But then how could the models detect the injections in the first place? Lederman and Mahowald suspected that the answers to Lindsey’s first question might have a more mundane origin as well. But after subjecting the models to a battery of tests, the researchers found that these simpler explanations couldn’t fully account for the models’ behavior. They’d come in as skeptics but encountered an effect they couldn’t explain away.

Taken together, the pair’s experiments suggested that models can detect when something unusual happens in their internal processing, but not specific details about the unusual activity. Lederman and Mahowald called this ability “anomaly detection.”

While anomaly detection isn’t as dramatic as the models’ evocative descriptions of injected concepts, it’s still striking in its own right. When training a model, researchers never tamper with its neural activity — so there’s no reason to expect it to develop the ability to detect this kind of tampering. Yet that’s what seems to have happened.
“The fact that it can notice the anomaly is insane,” Lederman said. “That is a mind-bending fact. It is wild, and it does seem robust to our various controls.”

Around the same time, Lindsey and his colleagues at Anthropic conducted a follow-up study focused on mapping out how this anomaly detection actually works, and they reached a similar conclusion. Other researchers have continued to explore alternative “deflationary” explanations using smaller models, but it remains to be seen whether they can account for all the results of Lindsey’s experiments.

“It could be that there’s some maximally deflationary explanation for everything that’s going on,” said Jacob Andreas, a language model researcher at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “But if there is, I don’t think we’ve actually identified it yet.”

The bigger, thornier question is whether anomaly detection should count as introspection. In some respects it more closely resembles a sort of bodily reflex. But the distinction between physical and mental phenomena becomes murky in disembodied entities like language models.

“If you say, ‘Oh, I just cut you, can you notice?,’ that’s not introspection,” Lederman said. “If your only organ is the brain, and I cut you there and you notice, it’s unclear whether we should count that as introspection.”

In a spring 2026 paper, Ravfogel and his NYU colleagues Shashwat Singh and Tal Linzen raised an even broader philosophical concern with how language model researchers seek evidence of introspection. Intuitively, we think of introspection as a model’s ability to sense its internal states. But everything that happens inside a language model (after the very first step of reading an input) boils down to processing internal states. “If we say that this is introspection, the term ‘introspection’ becomes kind of meaningless,” Ravfogel said.

He and his colleagues argue that tests of introspection in language models should take inspiration from the leading theories of how introspection works in humans. In one prominent theory, the defining feature of introspection is that it’s based on particular mental representations of other thoughts. According to this view, thinking about apples involves a direct, or “first-order,” mental representation of the concept “apples,” while introspective awareness of your own thoughts involves a “second-order” mental representation, such as “I’m thinking about apples.” But when it comes to how concepts are represented in a language model — or a human brain, for that matter — it’s surprisingly tricky to draw a sharp distinction between first-order and second-order representations.

“Going down to a mechanistic level and probing the internals of a large language model makes you realize that that distinction is actually quite fuzzy, and maybe it’s fuzzy in humans as well,” said Steve Fleming, a neuroscientist at University College London who studies introspection in humans. “Cognitive scientists were in this illusory comfort zone.”

To some researchers, then, the most exciting aspect of the new line of work is the potential it offers to explore how humans think. Language models offer “a kind of sandbox for studying what sorts of mechanisms, what sorts of pressures, might have led to human introspective capacity,” Lederman said.

But translating insights from language model studies to human psychology involves significant conceptual hurdles. It’s not even obvious how the basic distinction between “self” and “other” that we take for granted translates to language models — two copies of the same language model are identical to a degree that’s unimaginable in humans. Language model introspection, if there is such a thing, may not look anything like introspection in humans.
“The notion of identity becomes very complicated, and I think identity is at the heart of introspection,” Andreas said. “It’s tempting to draw all kinds of analogies that I think just don’t hold.”

articles.title: Methodical/mercurial
paragraphs: How would it be if you woke up one morning around 4 am, consumed by an idea that felt like the Best Idea You Ever Had. You spend the next two hours fervently researching said idea, watching videos, reading in-depth articles, compiling a spreadsheet comparing costs, techniques and options, then buying a whole load of books and equipment, and signing up to courses to teach you how to bring this fantastic, life-changing idea to fruition. You book a viewing for the new house in a new country that you are going to buy after investigating climate, housing options and work opportunities. You book the flights for that trip, to a Pacific island, where you will learn to scuba dive and set up a business as a dive instructor having fully understood the tourism industry and its legal implications. You sign up for that master’s programme in hypnotherapy/mushroom-growing/road-building after comparing the cost and quality of all colleges offering these courses. Your research is deep, your conclusions well justified. These are all good choices.

Buzzing on your own brilliance at finding the answer to all of your problems, your true calling in life and, basically, frigging nirvana, you are desperate to wake your beloved, who is lying beside you, blissfully unaware that their world is about to be rocked. You think about waking them because you can’t contain all this excitement alone and need to share it, but it’s only 6 am and you know from experience that this wouldn’t end well. So you sit, fidgeting, watching the clock until 6:30 am. Surely, that’s late enough? Perhaps if you bring them coffee, they won’t be so mad. Yet how could they be mad, when what you’re about to reveal to them will make them say: ‘Why didn’t you wake me up sooner, you genius?’

But as you sit impatiently waiting for an acceptable hour to rouse your beloved and blow their mind, your whole self shifts sideways, like someone just turned the TV over to another channel or a changeling took over your mind. You suddenly realise that your previously designated Best Idea Ever is full of holes and is actually a Terrible Idea. You are puzzled that you didn’t see this sooner. What were you thinking? You can’t move house because your kids are in school here, you have a full-time job and bills to pay, and you don’t have the attention span to read your horoscope, let alone do a master’s. And you can’t even swim.

What idiot thought that any of this was a good idea? Oh… it was me. OK… time to cancel it all and hope that you didn’t lose too much money and that it will all be back in the bank account before ‘they’ wake up.
And hope that you don’t do the same thing again tonight.

You will likely have come across the term AuDHD used as a shortcut to describe those given the dual diagnosis of autism and attention-deficit and hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). It is a relatively new label and for good reason – until recently, no one individual was clinically permitted to be given both diagnoses and therefore there was no one to whom the term ‘AuDHD’ could officially apply.

In 1994, a mere 32 years ago, the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th edition (DSM-IV), included Asperger Syndrome for the first time. In 2013, the diagnosis was removed from the 5th edition (DSM-5) and subsumed under the broader category of ‘autism spectrum disorder’. Asperger Syndrome had identified individuals who met the social and behavioural aspects of the diagnostic criteria for autism but who did not have intellectual disability or the language-development differences then associated with an autism diagnosis. As a result, an autistic person reading this magazine today would have been unlikely to receive an autism diagnosis in the past: there was simply no diagnostic category that fit their profile. That helps to explain the huge rise in adult diagnoses in recent decades.

Alongside this, diagnosis of ADHD in adults has been a similarly recent arrival. Having been considered a predominantly childhood condition for most of its history, the idea that children can continue to experience ADHD features into adulthood was not seriously considered until the early 2000s. Earlier versions of the DSM required that symptoms had to have been present prior to the age of seven years, and focused almost entirely on childhood behaviours to form the diagnosis. In 2013, with the publication of the DSM-5, the onset age of ADHD symptoms was raised to 12 years, and fewer symptoms were required for adults to meet the diagnostic threshold – which took into account development changes and challenges within adult settings, such as work – thus opening up ADHD diagnosis to adults.

This means that a person without intellectual disability and with relatively typical language development has been eligible for an autism diagnosis for only 32 years. And the ADHD criteria have been explicitly adapted to better recognise the disorder in adults only since 2013. That history is one part of the AuDHD issue.

The second part is that autism and ADHD were long considered mutually exclusive. It was thought that their apparently contradictory traits of rigidity and impulsivity effectively cancelled each other out. This meant that a person – either child or adult – could not be officially diagnosed with both conditions until 13 years ago, when the DSM-5 removed this exclusion and allowed both diagnoses to be given to the same person – opening the way for what is now widely called AuDHD.

At first glance, existing diagnostic criteria for each condition may look like contradictions of each other. While a stereotypical autistic person may present as socially awkward, precise and cautious in language and behaviour, requiring predictability, sameness and calm, our ADHDer looks like the complete opposite. ADHD diagnostic criteria typically present as someone socially driven, scattered and impulsive in language and behaviour, seeking novelty, variety and stimulation. How can it be that both of these seemingly opposing traits can exist in one person, and what is it like for that person when they do?

Given the relatively recent formal recognition of this comorbid profile, research into its impact is unsurprisingly scarce and, aside from a small handful of papers, has been focused on children and adolescents. The earliest research into this overlap I could find was published in 1999; those investigators concluded that autistic features were common in those with ADHD, and that a dual diagnosis should be considered in some cases, even though this was not clinically permitted at the time. This overlap has been one of the most frequently studied aspects of AuDHD.

A 2023 systematic review identified 9,050 articles and ultimately included 23 studies; across these, estimates of the prevalence of ADHD symptoms in autistic young people without intellectual disability ranged from 2.6 per cent to 95.5 per cent. Another paper suggested that 50 to 70 per cent of autistic people present with comorbid ADHD. If you are reading this article with a diagnosis of autism or ADHD, you may want to think about whether you may be both, because it’s looking increasingly likely that you are.

Of course, there have always been differing opinions and concerns about the pathologising nature of diagnosis in neurodiversity. Where does one neurodivergent condition end and another begin? Can we really separate these aspects of ourselves into neat clinical categories – often deemed necessary to permit access to a particular support service, therapy, fund or setting to meet the often-disabling needs of being neurodivergent in a neurotypical world? The reality is that no one knows the answers, so here we are with our rigid clinical diagnostic criteria, which – as we can see from the alterations in the DSM-5 – are changing as understanding grows. Forgive me for working within these uncomfortable neat boxes, but they are all we have right now; and, for at least some people, they can be a helpful way of understanding the contradictions of living with AuDHD.

The example at the top of the article is one from my own life and it has resonated with many of the 69 AuDHD adults and parents of AuDHD children whose stories and words I had the privilege to gather for my new book, The Complete Guide to AuDHD (2026).

My own AuDHD story is a typical one. I was diagnosed as autistic in my 40s after having written five books on autism and neurodiversity and achieving an MA in autism – I knew my stuff, and myself, or at least I thought I did. Yet I had led a chaotic life of multiple jobs, house moves and plans and schemes of one kind or another – I am known for it by those who know me; they take bets on how long I will stay in one place/job/course/project – which upsets me, but which is hard, logically, to take umbrage at.

I had never considered that I would meet the criteria for ADHD diagnosis because I was too logical, too organised and too set in my ways. I am the Queen of the Spreadsheet, the Mistress of the Plan. After bringing up two kids, I worked as a trainer and speaker for 15 years, travelling the country and overseas on a crazy schedule of driving, hotels and public speaking. Not surprisingly, I crashed horribly into years of panic attacks, agoraphobia and severe physical and mental burnout. Eventually, I gave it all up and began working locally and remotely, removing 90 per cent of the stress and unpredictability of my former life. At first, it was wonderful, I remembered what it was like to wake up without a brick of dread and anxiety on my chest. I slept in the same bed every night and knew what each day would bring. Perfect. Until… a few weeks into this blissful new existence I recall a feeling that I verbalised at the time as ‘I feel like I’m dead.’ I felt flat, blank, nothing, emotionless. Over a period of reflection, I realised that I had never actually sat still my whole life. While my former parenting and working lives had failed to meet my autistic need for routine and predictability, they had entirely satisfied – what I now understood to be – my ADHD need for constant dopamine in the form of novelty, variety and excitement.

Those who have the same experience of a second diagnosis of either autism or ADHD share the same feeling I did – it’s the final piece of the puzzle. The first diagnosis made sense of a lot, but it didn’t explain it all. There were questions and gaps: ‘I’m too social to be autistic.’ ‘I need too much order to be ADHD.’

Since the dual diagnosis of the two conditions is fairly recent, it is still unusual for both diagnoses to occur at the same time, with most adults currently having received one diagnosis first and the second at some point later, as did I. And although autism and ADHD were deemed contradictory for much of their joint history, both sets of diagnostic criteria need to be met for each diagnosis to be given: there is no allowance made for ADHD characteristics masking those of autism, for example – which they often do – during the diagnostic assessment.

Which diagnosis comes first varies from person to person, with either autism or ADHD often appearing as the primary profile. Perhaps ADHD appears more ‘visible’ for a child challenged by sitting still at school, or autism for an adult struggling with the social and flexibility requirements of a job – with the other lurking behind ready to throw a spanner in the works or offer a helping hand. Given that the second diagnosis was simply not an option for so long, the thought of it was generally never given the time of day, although a number of AuDHD people I have assessed often say they’d felt that the first diagnosis had answered some of the questions they’d had throughout their lives about why they were different, but not all. For others, it was a complete surprise. As one person I interviewed for my book explained:

For many, this ‘primary’ profile is not fixed. Female hormones are known to affect the severity of ADHD. The time of day and associated stress and fatigue play a role. And the impact depends on the activity contemplated – does it require speed and creativity, or accuracy and focus?

The idea of the autistic and ADHD selves as separate entities is hardly definitive, and experts differ here. Some research finds autism and ADHD symptoms to be largely segregated along existing diagnostic boundaries; others that they have overlapping features; while others suggest that the co-occurrence of autism and ADHD may represent a distinct combined phenotype. Regardless of the thoughts of academics, this sense of two selves, of conflict and contradiction and the push and pull of opposing wants and needs, is one that formed the core and essence of the experience of the participants in my own research.

An article by Siân Boyle in The Guardian in 2024 described this contradiction in the AuDHD label as one of ‘oxymoronic nature, perpetual internal war and rollercoaster of needs’, which nicely sums things up.

The realisation that there is a name and an explanation for the persistent inconsistency that accompanies the AuDHD lived experience can be liberating – it’s a relief to know that you are not actually crazy, because that’s the way it can feel. In the words of my research participants, it is:

Despite this sense of contradiction, the two conditions do share some characteristics. Both are highly heritable and run through families. As far back as 2009, a team led by the child and adolescent psychiatrist Aisling Mulligan at Trinity College Dublin found that autistic traits in children with ADHD ran in families, along with the ADHD itself. More recent research shows that mothers with ADHD are six times more likely to have a child with ADHD – and 2.5 times as likely to have an autistic child. Other studies suggest a shared genetic base between autism and ADHD, explaining the high prevalence of both conditions in the same families. Twin studies provide further evidence of this genetic overlap.

People with either autism or ADHD may find it challenging to read subtle social nuances and engage in reciprocal conversation, making it harder to sustain friendships and relationships. Both often have intense passions and interests, although these tend to last longer in autism than in ADHD. And while sensory features are not mentioned in the diagnostic criteria for ADHD, both groups may have atypical sensory profiles. As a very broad generalisation, autistic people find sensory experiences overwhelming, leading them to avoid some sensations and seek out comfort. On the other hand, ADHD people may seek sensory input and stimulation to feel grounded and focused. Although it is early days for research and the number of papers looking at AuDHD are small and focused almost entirely on children and adolescents, the general consensus is that the combination of autism and ADHD makes things worse socially, adaptively, behaviourally and mentally. I could not find any research-based evidence that sought or found examples of the dual diagnosis making life better. It seems that, in academic studies, questions relating to the advantages and joys of AuDHD were not asked, and that the focus was entirely on problems, challenges and deficit, as is often, disappointingly, the case.

The inconsistency brought by these apparently opposing sets of features does cause considerable frustration for the typical AuDHDer, who lives switching – often rapidly – between seeking both order and disruption, sameness and variety, impulsivity and risk-aversion, social motivation and solitude, single focus and multi-focus. When needs and wants shift so quickly and vary so wildly, decision-making and balance can feel impossible, leading to a far more chaotic life than would be expected from someone with an autism diagnosis. As one of the research participants said:

Yet the participants in my own research reported the joys of AuDHD as well. For me, the combination of the detail and diligence of autism and the creativity and impulsivity of ADHD have likely led to my deeply interesting and varied life, because I couldn’t have tolerated it any other way. Every day needs to be filled with entertainment and stability, learning and fun. Others in my research agree:

For me, it feels like a life of two halves, like living as a pair of twins who argue a lot but now and again will sit on the couch together and watch a movie. We know we have to have a schedule, eat the same foods and get things done. We know we have to physically move – a lot – keep switching tasks, and force ourselves to stop when we’re just done. We know we find it hard to begin, hard to keep going and hard to stop, and we’re continually developing ways to work with all of that at any given time in all given circumstances.

And although Autism has to step in to keep ADHD in check, and force it to sit down and do the dull, important things for a few minutes – rather than spending all day watching videos about giant tortoises on the Galápagos Islands – ADHD also needs to break through the rigidity of Autism’s need for productivity, tell it to lighten up – and come watch some of these great videos on giant tortoises on the Galápagos Islands. And then, once ADHD has piqued Autism’s interest with today’s Best Idea Ever, Autism can become a world authority on tortoises, research the climate, food, cheapest flights and best hotel on the islands, and build a spreadsheet to get this trip on the road. What a team!
We only have to hope that Autism knows where the passport is.

articles.title: The Best Food Gifts Under $25 (That Feel Thoughtful and Chic)
paragraphs: Eater’s under-$25 holiday gift guide is, unabashedly, one of my favorites to curate during gift guide season — both as a shopping writer and a writer who lives, laughs, loves to shop. I live for the thrill of a thrifty find; that rush of finding the perfect gift that somehow comes in way under budget is a sensation I first experienced while thrifting with my mom as a kid, when I was taught to sniff out authentic English ironstone bowls like an Antiques Roadshow bloodhound. I have been John Wick-training for this moment.

The best gifts under $25 for the true food freaks in your life (including yourself) should speak to their specific culinary obsessions, tastebuds, and cult-fave restaurants. Keep an eye out for those limited-edition holiday gifts that are going to sell out soon, and, when you see a potential present, ask yourself: does it inspire whimsy? Why should I settle for a spoon rest that isn’t shaped like ravioli? Move those mugs and snacks from heritage and indie brands to the front of the line, and maybe even click add-to-cart twice so that you, too, can experience the magic of Spaghetti Dust.
Whether you’re looking for a White Elephant present or an offering to impress your in-laws, let’s shop for the best food- and drink-related gifts under $25.

Diaspora Spice Co. is one of my favorite places to buy spices online, because the selection is always exciting and the company pays its farm partners an average of six times more than the commodity price. This year’s enticingly versatile gingerbread spice blend caught my eye, because it can be used for baking, or for simply sprinkling over coffee for a festive boost. Bundle it up with a nice velvet bow and a highly specific, nostalgic thrift-store mug for a delightful gift.

The wonder elicited from this traveling tube of “Spaghetti Dust” — aka ready-to-sprinkle dried garlic, Calabrian chile flakes, parsley, and sea salt — with its groovy graphics and gift-ready packaging, makes it one of the coolest food-themed presents that’s sure to sell out this holiday season. Just add olive oil and al dente pasta, and you’re ready to eat a delicious meal.

There’s something so comforting about a stoneware mug — holding one makes me feel instantly more cozy and learned, like a Nancy Meyers character rediscovering joy in an English countryside cottage. The ceramic material makes stoneware a great insulator when it comes to heat retention (without burning your hands), and this rustic, splatter stoneware mug from Hudson Grace is a looker.

Your giftee has all the deep-cut Kewpie mayonnaise flavors. They might even own the Kewpie cookbook. Now, give them the gift of a Kewpie mayo ornament to solidify their fealty to the Japanese mayo brand.

Ya Albi is a Palestinian American, mother-daughter-owned company that sources its slightly sweet, full-bodied olive oil from the West Bank, and packages it all in a chic pink tin. Plus, all of the oil’s proceeds go toward HEAL Palestine, a nonprofit organization that supports Palestinian children impacted by the war on Gaza. (To shop for even more Palestinian olive oils, check out this Eater guide.)

Technically, it’s 20 cents over our $25 budget, but this princess cake-inspired soap from Flamingo Estate is too good to pass up. The soap is made by whipping together shea butter and raspberry oil, and perfumed with a combination of scents like sweet almond, heliotrope blossoms, and musky amber to create a marzipan and cream-esque olfactory profile. The bar is then given a final romantic garnish, and elegantly engraved with its prinsesstårta namesake.

From traditional, sprawling brasseries to the incoming wave of Parisian global gastronomy, Eater has you covered for dining out in the City of Lights with The Eater Guide to Paris. Whether your giftee is planning an upcoming trip to Paris or an aspirational one, this trusty tome is filled with vetted Eater favorites for every kind of hungry traveler.

It’s always a bonus when you find a gift with packaging so stunning that it’s already gift-ready. Pastiglie Leone is a heritage Italian confectionery whose candies make a perfect stocking stuffer, host gift, or present for the person in your life who owns a silver-plated toast rack and goes to high tea at least once a year.
For the home cook who also loves to journal, I suggest a fresh batch of snack-centric stickers. What better way is there to bookend a day than with a sticker spread featuring Pocky and Heineken beer?
