articles.title: How Did Nathan Fielder Pull This Off?
paragraphs: Sometimes simply stating a fact helps to underline just how unusual it sounds. Last weekend, the biggest movie in America was a nearly three-hour documentary. Yes, You Can See Everything is a special kind of film, featuring a “star,” of sorts, in the comedian Nathan Fielder and a notorious public figure as its subject in Elizabeth Holmes. But there’s no need to really split hairs on this. To make a documentary the must-see release of the fall is a stunning achievement—for Fielder; for his co-director, Lance Oppenheim; and for the distributor, A24.

You Can See Everything’s $11.4 million haul over Halloween weekend helped it climb to No. 1, dethroning the DC Comics adaptation Clayface; in the three weeks since its release, it has earned some $64 million and counting. That makes it one of the highest-grossing documentaries of all time, behind only some museum-friendly nature features; concert films by Michael Jackson, Justin Bieber, and Taylor Swift; and Michael Moore’s Fahrenheit 9/11. (In the case of the latter, which earned more than $200 million worldwide: Talk about another distinct cultural moment.) Fielder made a name for himself on cable TV; he first won acclaim with the Comedy Central series Nathan for You. But he followed that up with more avant-garde works, namely The Curse (on Showtime) and HBO’s The Rehearsal. Moving from those to mainstream movie stardom would be a difficult step for most; Fielder has done it while retaining his deadpan on-screen personality.

Fielder’s name brand aside, his documentary’s unusual success can’t be attributed to one particular thing. The continued public interest in the Elizabeth Holmes case certainly helps. The story of her failed company, Theranos, is an ongoing topic of fascination, despite not producing much news in recent years; the 2022 Hulu miniseries The Dropout boosted its visibility. You Can See Everything’s rave reviews, of course, also matter a lot—as much as industry folk occasionally love to claim that film criticism has gone extinct, discourse can help draw attention to more commercially risky projects like this one.

A24, which often does an excellent job conceiving its projects’ publicity campaigns, also came up with an unusually good release strategy for the documentary. You Can See Everything’s premiere was a genuine surprise at the Telluride Film Festival—although I had heard plenty of chatter that something was going to screen there last-minute, the company really kept all the details locked down. Even after the cat was out of the bag, the buzz around the documentary remained mystical and secretive, with hints that it had a major “twist.” Spoilers abound for those who haven’t seen it yet: The actor Amanda Seyfried appears in the movie’s latter half, brought in by the co-directors because of her experience playing Holmes in The Dropout. She not only reprises her performance, but also functions as both an audience surrogate and a fresh pair of eyes on Fielder’s relationship with the disgraced biotech entrepreneur; together, they puzzle out the extent to which he might have been manipulated.

Essentially, A24 (and Fielder and Oppenheim) managed to turn a documentary into a narrative event. It feels like a scripted film, with a protagonist who experiences a complex arc—a rare achievement for the form. Its success, which has given birth to numerous think pieces, memes, and Halloween costumes, is bound to breathe new life into a somewhat commercially moribund medium. The last wave of theatrically released nonfiction sensations came in the late 2010s, led by (smaller-size) box-office hits such as Won’t You Be My Neighbor? and RBG. By and large, breakout entries have focused on either celebrities or true-crime cases. Many of the biggest releases are now relegated to streaming; Netflix, in particular, has become a real powerhouse in the genre. Following the coronavirus pandemic, fewer and fewer documentaries have received theatrical rollouts, and the market for them at film festivals has slumped.

A rebound, however, seems likely. Other well-received nonfiction movies are circulating in theaters: John Wilson’s brilliant The History of Concrete, a feature-length version of the wry stylistic schtick he presented in his HBO show, sold out screens in New York City its opening weekend. Naza, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s searing follow-up to the Oscar-winning No Other Land, has been doing similarly robust business in indie cinemas; news reports that the Israeli government is looking to revoke the filmmakers’ citizenship (for interviewing IDF members about carrying out alleged war crimes) have likely contributed to growing interest. Alex Gibney’s sprawling Musk has also made headlines for the way it allegedly earned the ire of its subject, although the doc will likely perform better on streaming, given its four-hour runtime.

You Can See Everything, however, has transcended the art-house market that these other movies are playing in. Its performance also might be difficult for Hollywood to copy. Consider the staggering sensation Backrooms (another A24 film), which prompted studios to acquire other bits of YouTube horror in order to try to imitate its appeal for Gen Z viewers. Producers may struggle to find successors that replicate the weird alchemy of Fielder and Oppenheim’s project, which combined an alluring focus with their very specific, funny perspective. If this box-office smash just turns out to be a black-swan event for documentary filmmaking, it will be a fascinating one to remember—and either way, You Can See Everything’s success proves that audiences are interested in a broader set of theatrical fare than just superhero-heavy lineups.
When a Movie Hinges on a Kid’s Performance

Josephine is anchored by Mason Reeves, the actor who plays Josephine, who was 8 at the time of filming. Her performance sensitively conveys her character’s mixture of confusion, frustration, fear, and curiosity. Reeves is now 10, and she’s been enthusiastic, Beth Araújo told me, about acting in another project soon. Araújo would rather she didn’t. “I hope and I believe Mason had a great experience on this,” she told me in September, “and I hope she also puts it aside for a while.”

Oscar season is really about to kick off. November is when the slow rollout of high-profile releases start choking movie theaters, typically first in a few locations in New York and Los Angeles. But Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine will make a bigger debut this Friday ahead of a major Oscar campaign. If you enjoy McDonagh’s acidic brand of dramedy, this film will work for you—it’s witty, mordant, and cynical, with delightful cursing variants and extremely well-acted performances by its two leads, John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell. It follows two jaded CIA operatives (Malkovich and Rockwell) vacationing on Easter Island, shortly before the 1973 coup d’etat that brought Pinochet to power in Chile; the shaggy moral quality recalls McDonagh’s best film, In Bruges, in which a pair of lost souls wrestle (humorously) with the limits of their villainy. Malkovich is doing especially soulful work that may earn him an Oscar. But my overall opinion on Wild Horse Nine is firmly “good, not great”; it’s a bit of a retread after the heights of McDonagh’s previous movie, the excellent The Banshees of Inisherin.

Another prestige-y newcomer is Godzilla Minus Zero, the follow-up to the critically acclaimed, Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One. Explaining the many strands of Godzilla is hard: The character has appeared in films for several decades and across multiple continuities, including an extant (and successful) American offshoot that will receive another entry next year. (In that sequel, Godzilla once again does battle alongside King Kong.) But Minus Zero, directed by Takashi Yamazaki, furthers the rebooted myth from Minus One, which laid out a more grounded narrative for the legendary kaiju. Both are period pieces that recontextualize Godzilla as a monster that emerges in the aftermath of World War II and subsequent nuclear testing, echoing the character’s ’50s origins. Minus Zero effectively ups the disaster scale and looks incredible; if you liked Minus One, as I did, you’ll certainly like this one too.

October was horror month, and I love to tackle franchises I have never fully filled in. This year I took on The Ring, watching all four of the original Japanese films (assembled in a lovely box set by the distributor Arrow Video), including the bizarre and forgotten side-sequel Spiral. Then I tackled Gore Verbinski’s stunning American remake of the first film; the truly bizarre The Ring Two (directed by Hideo Nakata, who made the original Japanese Ringu); and the reprehensibly bad reboot Rings. Nothing more fun than riding the ups and downs of a horror series!

articles.title: Import AI 479: Spacewar; low-latency tasks versus LLMs; Genie 4
paragraphs: LLMs are very bad at low-latency tasks: …Realtime-Bench says it’ll be a while till AI systems can play games or do online auctions for you… Researchers have built Realtime-Bench, “a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success”. The test helps evaluate how well modern, general-purpose AI systems can perform tasks where decisions need to be made in real-time. The benchmark consists of 50 interactive game and web tasks, split across 30 web tasks in four categories (travel, e-commerce, service, and security), and 20 game tasks (arcade, puzzle, strategy, and simulation). Who did the research: The benchmark was built by people at the University of Texas at Austin, Ohio State University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, NVIDIA, Northwestern University, and Steadyworks. What it measures: The test is designed to probe for three qualities: temporal state awareness (”RT-Perceive”), where models can use observations to track changes in the world; adaptive deliberation (”RT-Deliberate”), where models alter their reasoning length and depth according to available time; and time-aware action selection (”RT-Act”) where models need to appropriately time their actions for the situation. “For example, an agent purchasing a ticket must track the sale status and assess whether observed availability is still current (RT-Perceive), limit further deliberation when the purchase window is closing (RT-Deliberate), and choose between waiting for sales to open and purchasing while tickets remain available (RT-Act).” They have three different conditions: Wall clock, which is designed to test out performance under real-world latency. Paused clock, which lets you arbitrarily pause things so you can get a sense of baseline capability, and Token clock, which “advances the environment at a fixed rate per generation token. An action is applied at the simulated time reached when it is committed, so consuming more tokens delays execution regardless of actual inference latency”. How well do models do? The authors tested out models from OpenAI (GPT-6-Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-Realtime-2, OpenAI Decisions), Anthropic (Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5), Google (Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, Gemini 3.8 Live), Jev 1.13, as well as Chinese models from Deepseek (V4.1) and Moonshot AI (Kimi-K3). GPT-6 Astra (high) got the highest pass rate on the ‘wall clock’ evaluation setting, with 36%. By comparison, with a paused clock, models with high reasoning get closer to 70% or even 80% success. Why this matters: This benchmark is an effective proxy for where AI agents will break - the low scores here point to tasks where AI agents cannot yet be expected to perform well. Check out the leaderboard: Realtime-Bench (official website). Read the paper: Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems? (arXiv). *** The future of spacewar, courtesy of the Defense Intelligence Agency: …Anti-satellite tech, space nukes, and more… Working in AI can be stressful so sometimes to relax myself I like to read about other topics to get a sense for what horrors lie elsewhere. I take the same approach with depression, where if I feel sad I will try and listen to music by people sadder than me in an attempt to cheer myself up (e.g., Radiohead, Neil Young, and in very dark moments Bill Callahan / Smog, etc). So with that in mind I recently read “Challenges to Security in Space”, by the Defense Intelligence Agency. What’s going on in space: As with conflict on Earth, space is defined by conflict between the US versus China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, with China the most technologically sophisticated, and Russia the most seemingly gung ho. “China and Russia are developing a formidable spectrum of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations,” the DIA writes. “China has more than tripled its space launches per year in the past decade, with 22 launches in 2016 and 93 launches in 2025… Beijing judges space is central to the United States and its allies’ operations. Beijing also considers space an offensive military domain, which has shaped integral components of PLA military planning and campaigns.” Spacewar: The general vibe you get from reading this 100+ page report is there is a huge amount of ugly, frightening stuff happening in space, or being done to things in space by things on the ground. Some example quotes:
“By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits”
“China is developing space-based technology, including on-orbit counterspace weapons, capable of holding space systems at risk”
“Russia’s Peresvet, a ground-based laser system, is designed to dazzle enemy satellites’ optical systems to mask the movement of Russia’s strategic missile systems”

“Russia has launched several satellites over the last few years which conducted test activities on orbit for technologies that could enable attacks on other countries’ satellites and result in temporary or permanent damage”

China has a couple of spaceplanes, akin to the US’s hyper-secret X-37B vehicle, and they appear to be getting more sophisticated. In 2023, one of China’s aforementioned vehicles, “released and interacted with an object.”
Satellite-on-satellite fights: It’s obvious throughout the report that we’re in a world where rival nations have satellites that try to go up and mess with other satellites from other people.

“In 2019, Russia launched satellite Cosmos 2542, which released a second satellite, Cosmos 2543. Cosmos 2543 then began following a U.S. national security satellite and approached it multiple times at a distance close enough to create potentially dangerous operating conditions,” the DIA writes. “Russia is developing kinetic orbital systems to permanently disable, or “kill,” satellites. Moscow’s Burevestnik is a developmental, co-orbital air-launched ASAT weapon for killing spacecraft in LEO”.

“In February 2022, Russia launched a satellite called Cosmos, which Moscow claimed at the time was testing the effects of space radiation on electronic systems. This satellite was launched into an unusual and isolated orbit not used by any other spacecraft”.

Space nukes: Russia is experimenting with nukes in space. “A nuclear detonation in space would create an electromagnetic pulse, which would immediately affect satellites within range and could impact civilian infrastructure,” the DIA writes. “A nuclear detonation in space could be tailored to impact satellites in most orbits—LEO for commercial and reconnaissance satellites, GEO for critical communications, and MEO for navigation and timing satellites”. Why this matters - infrastructure for the next phase of the AI power struggle: As people spend more resources on building space-based data centers (and eventually, perhaps, lunar-based ones), space will become ever more strategically and commercially valuable and ever more contested. Research like this gives us a sense of the hardware which is already in space and will arrive in the future. Perhaps in some far-off future an AI might seek to take control of such space assets as well. Read more: DIA Releases Challenges to Security in Space (Defense Intelligence Agency, press release). Read the report: Challenges to Security in Space (DIA, PDF). *** Metis: A startup trying to fuse symbolic and neural reasoning: …Towards Vulcan-like machine minds… Metis, a startup that wants to build novel AI architectures oriented around developing machines with better reasoning, has published a research paper laying out its research approach. The high-level summary is simple - Metis wants to do for modern open-domain problems what DeepMind did for closed-domain problems like board games via its work on AlphaGo and AlphaGo Zero. What they want to do: The key idea here is to add a reasoning core to modern AI architectures which is far more reliable than what we have today. “In modern AI architectures much of the other surrounding machinery that made AlphaGo a successful reasoning system remains either implicit or absent,” they write. “The first missing element is an explicit and persistent epistemic state… the second missing element is a criterion that allows the system to choose reasoning moves that make progress towards the goal.” This is more of a position paper than a technical paper, so they don’t have a ton of detail here. The main idea is to train a reasoning policy and value function based on real-world data collection, then use this to guide the system to perform reasoning that reduces long-term uncertainty, and have these sit on a basic core of data made up of claims or hypotheses about the world. “Any change to a claim’s evidential status must be licensed by evidence or verified through explicit calculation and approved by an independent judgment system,” they write. “Model-generated content cannot enter the accepted epistemic state merely by being plausible; it must pass warrant assessment, which lowers hallucinations. Sources of evidence can be attached directly to the propositions they support, providing a clear chain of provenance. The reasoning process becomes explicitly auditable.” Why this matters - building reliable substrates that are also deeply inhuman: Ideas like the architecture described here are fascinating both because of the promise they bring for increasing the reliability of AI systems, but also for how deeply inhuman they are: humans do not reason from some pristine base of facts, rather it’s all a big messy blob of memory and intuitions and some rules (some of which are learned from experience and some of which seem more platonic, like forms of logical reasoning). In this way, contemporary LLMs are more like humans than the system described here. “While the history of AI can be understood as a contest between symbolic and neural methods, it may be more constructive to view it as a story of two incomplete successes,” Metis writes. “Classical systems made aspects of the reasoning process explicit but depended on representations, operators, heuristics and knowledge supplied largely by hand. Contemporary LLMs learn extraordinary semantic operations and vast bodies of implicit knowledge but leave the organisation, evaluation and accumulation of reasoning implicit.” The AI system described here would ‘think’ in a way that is very different to how humans think and such a system might show us more about the differences between our own intelligence and that of machines. Read more: The Age of Reasoning (Metis, PDF). *** Google summons Genie 4 for better world modeling: …One of Google’s most interesting projects continues to live!... Google DeepMind has published details on Genie 4, a new iteration of its Genie world model. The company is rolling out access to Genie 4 currently as a research preview for some trusted testers and will eventually come to Google AI Ultra subscribers. The Genie series of models are fascinating, showing a world where you can take a photograph of anything and turn it into an interactable environment, or one where you can convert a 2D drawing into the stage for a videogame, and more. Key features: Google calls out four features that make Genie 4 different to previous ones. These include:

Real-time modification: “You can use natural language to modify a simulation in real-time — like changing the weather, moving the camera, or introducing a new person or object — and Gemini will contextually adapt your prompt to match the surrounding scene.”

Physics and human action simulation: “Genie 4 simulates real-world physics scenarios, such as aerodynamics, collisions, and more,” and it also simulates people better. “The most dramatic leap is how Genie 4 simulates people, creating characters that move naturally, respond organically to their environments, and can be interactively steered in real-time.”
Sound modeling: “Genie 4 is our first real-time world model to generate audio natively,” Google writes. It also “introduces interactive dialogue that adapts on the fly.”

Simulating complex events: Google has embedded Gemini 3.8 Flash into Genie 4, so that the fast Flash model “serves as a guiding agent in the loop”, providing continual calibration. “Gemini continuously observes the scene, breaks down goals into a sequence of steps, and reviews incoming frames to track the progress and verify that each step succeeded. As the world shifts or the user intervenes, Gemini adapts its plan in the moment, unlocking worlds with reliable causality, procedural behaviors, and multi-step reasoning.”

Why this matters - towards a multitude of worlds all dreamed up by machines: Though the technology is currently quite janky (e.g., robotic voices, a dreamlike sort of inconsistency in the visualized environments, etc), it points towards a world where we can generate infinite forms of entertainment (and potentially data?) via creating and prompting custom worlds. Read the announcement post: Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation (Google DeepMind blog). Watch the video: Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation (Google DeepMind, YouTube). Tech Tales: City Race [Description of a game played in the 2040s] One of the favorite games that children would play after The Uplift was called City Race; in it, they competed against one another to plan, build, and manage cities, expanding across the domain of a novel planet. The cities were trapped in time, starting with the technology of whatever era they were in, and the games took place over the course of about a century, allowing some further technology development to occur. Each game was played using a slice of the resources from the Dyson Swarm, allowing for a powerfully complex simulation (albeit with local-agent cognitive gating, such that nothing could develop enough sophistication to be deemed a Conscious Entity). Hundreds of thousands of simulated minds lived and died, sometimes thriving in cities run by careful and effective owners, and other times trapped in squalor, or growing old in places whose economies were hollowing out; casualties of the successes of others. It was deemed good for the children to learn what it meant to be gods, before they became adults. At the closure of every game, the children would need to spend a day living inside each of the cities in the gameworld they had played; those who had built marvelous cities experienced the wonders of their own creation, then walked through the broken towns whose success had been stymied by their own. Those who had struggled lived in their twilight towns, then got to tour the far off places that had doomed them.
Things that inspired this story: Player of Games by Iain M Banks; Simcity; game playing; urban design; The Glass Bead Game by Hermann Hesse. Thanks for reading!

articles.title: Software engineering at Google & CS education with Titus Winters
paragraphs: An engineer who helped create today’s software engineering curriculum now says to burn down almost all of it. What’s the cause of this contradiction? We find out from the lead author of Software Engineering at Google.

Titus Winters spent more than a decade at Google, where he led its readability program and built Abseil, Google’s open-sourced foundational C++ libraries. He is currently a Senior Principal Scientist at Adobe, where he focuses on developer experience and productivity.

In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Titus and I discuss how his team tackled a massive refactoring project across Google’s 250-million-line C++ codebase, why Google made testing mandatory, and his work on updating the ACM/IEEE undergraduate computer science curriculum guidelines.
We also explore why traditional productivity metrics miss some of AI’s biggest benefits, what needs to change in CS education, and how new engineers can stand out.
Titus is a deep thinker and has worked on some very interesting projects. Here are 12 things that stick out to me from our chat.

1. Was refactoring 250M+ lines of C++ code the largest refactoring task of all time? This happened at Google in 2010, a few months after Titus joined the search giant. An internal email asked for volunteers to help clean up old C++ code, some of it written by the very first Googlers.

A team of a dozen people was assembled. Google had close to 250M lines of code at the time, edited by 10,000 engineers. Titus recalled the cleanup: “We were replacing the foundation of the Empire State Building. We were not allowed to close the building or block traffic. Oh, and we discovered nuclear waste in the basement.”
2. The refactoring was done with advanced language parsing techniques, long before LLMs existed. Back in 2010, there were no LLMs for this giant refactor. Here’s what the team did:
Parse: ran a MapReduce over the whole codebase. The mapper parsed every build target into an abstract syntax tree
Match: match exact call patterns in the tree
Code generation: generated edits to be made by the machine
Coexist: make the old API and new API work side-by-side
Shard: once the new API is ready to go, split the edits by directory, and send them out in batches
Block the old: make sure nobody copied the old pattern back into the code
The clang-format toolkit exists because Titus and his team needed it for this refactor.

3. Google made automated tests mandatory after Search could no longer ship regularly. Around 2007, Search, the flagship product, was unable to ship at a monthly cadence any more, and the best they could ship to production was quarterly.

Almost every change at Google touched Search’s code, even things like a change to Gmail. To clamp down, Google, as an org, mandated that every change was to be accompanied by a test. Over time, Search returned to its former higher cadence.
4. Google’s readability program might have been the largest educational program ever in tech. To make a code change at Google, two people need to sign off that change through a code review:
An “owner” of the file/project: someone on the team with domain knowledge
A “readability” reviewer: an engineer certified to be a “readability” expert in the given language that the change was made in

Google’s first engineer, Craig Silverstein, walked each new dev hire through their first change. Java teams turned this approach into mentoring, where experienced reviewers were assigned to review all changes in a round-robin fashion. And soon enough, a formalized readability program was built for all languages. When Titus left Google three months ago, 10,000+ engineers were enrolled in readability at any given time. Has there ever been a bigger engineering “classroom” anywhere else?

5. Fear is not an acceptable basis for engineering. Titus believes your codebase is unsustainable if it’s not possible to make a valuable change safely. There shouldn’t be fear about making a change to a codebase. Having the right “security nets” that catch errors is strategically very valuable because it enables teams to make changes without fear.

6. With AI, outages seem to be going up. Titus talks to engineers at other companies and it’s the same picture: code output is up hugely versus a year ago, and outages are also up about 30%, while the number of features shipped is static. It seems like treading water. From that angle, it’s not positive for AI; based on outages alone, the technology could be a negative.

7. On the other hand, AI makes ambitious projects possible that weren’t realistic without it. Titus is optimistic about AI as a net productivity boost, and reckons people are caring about the wrong things. He sees the real value of AI as not in repeating the same things as before at higher speed. Instead, it’s about doing things you never thought of before: projects so ambitious that they didn’t used to make sense!

8. Burn down the US undergrad CS curriculum (most of it). Titus was the only working engineer on the steering committee for the ACM/IEEE/AAAI CS curriculum guidelines in 2023, and believes the curriculum is hopelessly out of date. He accuses it of not having altered substantially since around 2000, while the industry has. Testing and verification are cited as mattering a lot more for new joiners, but they are absent from the curriculum.

Unless major changes are made to make it relevant, computer science enrollment could fall and software engineering programs that focus on practical dev skills will be attractive to students – this is Titus’s forecast.
9. “Middle group” of students struggle most with AI. Professors in CS programs tell Titus that students divide into three groups:
The best are better than ever and take full advantage of a patient, knowledgeable tutor, aka the AI
The middle: professors say that everyone below the “best” have collapsed: students below a B grade tend to not understand code at all
The weakest: they can catch up to the middle of the pack easier – mostly by producing slop with AI, though.

When I did a guest lecture at my alma mater, professors told me similar observations – how the “middle of the pack students,” by grades, have disappointingly low understanding of the subject, compared to former years.
10. Grading students’ prompts and tests is better than focusing on their code. Titus would focus on the thinking processes students put into building and validating software, not just the output.

11. “Remember Andrew’s axe” – advice for junior engineers. Andrew chops down a tree with an axe. Or did Andrew’s axe chop down the tree? Titus says Andrew is the one who did it, and the axe is only a tool for his will. Similarly with AI: it’s a tool for you to use, and anthropomorphizing this tool takes us out of that mindset.

12. To succeed, don’t copy what everyone else is doing! As our time came to an end, I asked Titus what he’d say to sophomore students. It’s a segment that did not make it into the podcast, but I’m adding it here!

“Most of my success in life has come from not doing the thing that everyone else is doing. It is really incredibly hard to stand out if you are just listening to what is a hot topic and chasing the same shiny thing that literally everyone else is doing.
My primary advice [is to] find something that you love that is not just the same thing that you assume is on everybody’s resume, and do a lot of that. Find a passion project, go really deep on it.

Like, ‘how do I use computing and AI vibe coded new generation techniques?’ ‘How do I solve this problem that matters a lot to me?’ ‘Or how do I express myself through a game or art?’ The more that you do [something] that’s uniquely you, the more that you stand out, and the more that you do, the more that you learn.”

articles.title: How TUI scales threat modeling for 100+ teams with Amazon Bedrock
paragraphs: When your security team has four engineers and your organization has over 100 digital product teams, threat modeling becomes a bottleneck fast. That was the challenge TUI faced. TUI operates across the travel and tourism industry with airlines, hotels, cruise ships, and local travel experiences. Our Platform & Engineering division needs security assessments to keep pace.

At TUI, each threat modeling session took 4–6 hours of manual work: reviewing architecture diagrams, mapping threats to internal standards, researching security issues, and documenting findings in Confluence. The team could complete only 3–4 sessions per month, leaving a constant backlog.

TUI needed threat modeling to become mandatory for every new service, not a luxury TUI reserved for the highest-priority projects. TUI built an AI-powered threat modeling system using Amazon Bedrock, collaborating with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center during a 10-week proof of concept (PoC) to develop and validate the architecture. Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service for building generative AI applications, and TUI used the Claude Sonnet 4.5 foundation model from Anthropic. TUI chose Amazon Bedrock for managed access to Claude Sonnet 4.5 without operating model infrastructure, its extended thinking support that the workflow uses for deeper analysis, and its integration with the AWS services already in TUI’s stack. TUI deployed the agentic workflow on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, part of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore runtime hosts the agent in production without provisioning or scaling infrastructure. After the PoC, TUI took the system to production within 30 days.
In this post, we describe how TUI built an agentic AI workflow for threat modeling, the iteration process that shaped the architecture, and the results after deployment.

TUI’s security engineering team followed a thorough but manual process: for each application, an engineer reviewed the architecture, identified threats using STRIDE methodology, mapped them to TUI Technology Standards, P&E-specific standards, and ISO 27001 controls, and documented findings in Confluence with Jira tickets.

With 100+ digital product teams and only 3–4 sessions possible per month, most teams waited weeks for their review. Security engineers also had varying levels of expertise across technology stacks, and there was no automated way to verify these standards were consistently applied to every assessment.

The solution extends AWS Threat Designer with TUI-specific capabilities through a serverless architecture deployed in the eu-central-1 (Frankfurt) AWS Region. Model availability varies by Region. For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock. Together, these services replace the manual review process with an automated workflow that applies TUI Technology Standards and P&E-specific standards consistently. The system uses the following key services:
Amazon Bedrock for threat analysis and generation using Claude Sonnet 4.5 from Anthropic, with configurable extended thinking budgets.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime for hosting the agentic workflow as a managed, serverless runtime. It runs the containerized LangGraph agent without provisioning or scaling infrastructure, supports long-running sessions that exceed typical function timeouts, and provides per-session isolation for concurrent threat models.
AWS Lambda for serverless backend compute with LangGraph workflow orchestration.
Amazon DynamoDB for workflow state management with resume capability.
Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for architecture diagram storage, TUI knowledge base, and web search cache.
AWS Amplify for the React front end with Amazon Cognito authentication.

The core is a LangGraph-based agentic workflow that processes architecture diagrams through several specialized nodes. Engineers upload one or more diagrams (for example, a high-level architecture alongside a detailed network topology), which the workflow converts to base64 to identify components and data flows. It then loads relevant security standards and generates threats with iterative refinement. The workflow runs gap analysis, optionally compares against a subject matter expert (SME) assessment, and assembles the final threat model with export options (PDF, JSON, or Confluence).

The following screenshot shows the submission wizard. Engineers provide a title, upload architecture diagrams, add optional context and assumptions, and select a reasoning depth based on architecture complexity. The entire setup takes approximately two minutes.

Once submitted, the system processes the architecture through each workflow node with real-time progress tracking. Engineers can monitor which phase is active and return to review results when processing completes.
TUI’s team didn’t arrive at the final design on day one. They iterated through several approaches, and each failure pointed toward the next improvement.

Attempt 1: Load everything into the prompt. The first approach loaded all 192 TUI security standards (338 KB) directly into the foundation model context. This failed immediately. Some individual standard documents run 20+ pages, and the combined content exceeded token limits before the foundation model could begin threat analysis.

Even with a subset of standards, the foundation model struggled to follow structured instructions. When asked to recommend only TUI-approved tools for mitigations, it would ignore the approved tool list and suggest generic alternatives. Too much contradictory information from different standards confused the model.

Attempt 2: Metadata-driven selection. The breakthrough came from treating the problem as a search and selection challenge rather than a prompt-loading exercise. Instead of loading all standards, the team pre-generated lightweight metadata for each document: keywords, component types, STRIDE categories, and a relevance score.

At runtime, the foundation model reviews this metadata (about 60 KB) and selects only the 16 most relevant standards for the specific architecture being analyzed. This reduced context from 338 KB to 21 KB, a 94% reduction, while maintaining coverage. The reduction is calculated from the metadata approach versus loading all standards directly.

The metadata approach fits the structure of TUI’s knowledge base: some documents are always mandatory (security guidelines, approved tools), while others apply only to certain architectures. The team also evaluated retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but with a bounded corpus of 192 standards, some mandatory regardless of the query, metadata-driven selection proved more predictable and easier to debug. RAG may complement it as the knowledge base grows.

The threat generation node is where the agentic behavior matters most. Rather than generating threats in a single pass, the system uses a Reason and Act pattern with a LangGraph subgraph. The agent has four tools at its disposal: adding threats, deleting threats, reading the current threat catalog, and running gap analysis.

The agent autonomously decides which tools to call and in what order. It generates an initial set of threats using STRIDE methodology, then reviews its own output against the loaded TUI standards. Each threat includes a title, description, affected component, and threat vector. It also assigns likelihood and impact scores using TUI’s risk matrix. Threats include recommended mitigations with TUI-approved tools and mapped ISO 27001 controls.

A tool budget system helps prevent the agent from generating indefinitely. After three threat-generation calls, the system forces a gap analysis. The agent must step back and assess what’s missing before generating more. This mimics how human security experts work: generate, review, identify gaps, fill them.

A validation node checks three conditions before the workflow can proceed: the threat catalog isn’t empty, all six STRIDE categories are covered, and gap analysis has been performed at least once. If a check fails, the agent receives specific feedback and loops back.

Based on TUI’s production data, the combination of iterative generation and gap analysis typically produces 40–60 threats per architecture, compared to the 30–40 that manual sessions identified. It also supports configurable extended thinking budgets, from 24K reasoning tokens for standard architectures up to 64K for complex systems.

Security threats evolve regularly. A threat model generated today needs to account for issues disclosed last week. The workflow integrates web search to fill gaps where TUI’s internal standards don’t cover specific technologies.

For every technology identified in the architecture (Keycloak, Kong, Redis, and so on), the system generates two search queries: one for known issues and one for hardening best practices. These queries target authoritative sources such as OWASP, NIST, and CWE databases. Before making an API call, it checks an Amazon S3-based cache with a 7-day time-to-live (TTL). Only technology component names are used for external searches. Architecture details and customer data are not included in queries.

The cache key uses a hash of the sorted component names, deliberately excluding foundation model-generated descriptions. Those descriptions vary slightly between runs even for the same diagram, which would reduce cache effectiveness.

Based on TUI’s monitoring data, the cache achieves a 70–80% hit rate because many TUI applications share core technologies. A cache hit returns results in under 100 milliseconds, compared to 2–3 seconds for a live search. TUI’s team evaluated multiple search providers during the PoC and designed the system with a pluggable provider architecture, allowing provider switching as capabilities evolve.

TUI’s security engineers don’t just use the system. They validate it. The workflow includes an optional node where engineers upload their own manually created threat assessment as a PDF. The workflow extracts threats using Claude, normalizes risk ratings to a standard scale (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL), and matches them against the AI-generated threats using semantic similarity.

When the AI and the SME disagree on a threat’s severity, the system flags the discrepancy with both ratings and the SME’s rationale. For example, the AI might rate a credential stuffing event (automated login attempts using unintended disclosure of credential databases) as HIGH while the SME rates it MEDIUM. Over time, these comparisons calibrate the system’s risk scoring and surface areas where the AI consistently over- or under-estimates risk.

The following screenshot shows an SME Comparison Alert for a credential stuffing threat. The system matched the AI-generated threat with a similar SME threat, compared both ratings (AI: High, SME: HIGH), and provided the SME’s rationale alongside a recommendation.
After the PoC handover, TUI’s team took the system from prototype to production-ready deployment in 30 days. The following results reflect the system’s performance in production.
*Based on TUI’s internal measurements comparing pre- and post-deployment performance.

The solution processes each architecture in the eu-central-1 Region, with data encrypted at rest using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) and in transit with TLS. Architecture diagrams and threat models are processed within the AWS infrastructure, helping TUI meet its data residency and security requirements.

The following screenshot shows the threat catalog, a card view of completed threat models. Each card displays the original architecture diagram, an AI-generated description, completion status, and threat counts by severity (red for high, yellow for medium, green for low).
Engineers can select a threat model to view a dashboard with four analytical views: threats by likelihood, threats by STRIDE category, threats by target asset, and threat sources.

“In the first four weeks after launch, 64 users registered and 19 unique creators produced 34 threat models with Threat Designer. What previously took one to two weeks per assessment is now available on demand. As of October 2026, adoption has grown to 255 registered users, 86 threat models, and 43 active creators, demonstrating that teams are embracing self-service security as part of their development workflow.”
— Marvin Jordan, Head of Technology for Security Platform and Practices, TUI

TUI’s experience shows that agentic AI workflows can address a real operational challenge in enterprise security: making thorough threat modeling fast enough to be mandatory. The combination of metadata-driven context selection, self-correcting threat generation, and intelligent caching allowed a four-person security team to support over 100 digital product teams. TUI achieved consistent, standards-aligned assessments at scale.
Looking ahead, TUI plans to expand the system with automated Jira ticket creation for mitigation tracking and integration with CI/CD pipelines for pre-deployment security checks.

You can get started with Amazon Bedrock to build AI-powered security workflows and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to deploy agentic applications in production. For hands-on guidance with your specific use case, connect with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center. To explore the open source foundation that this solution extends, see the Threat Designer project on GitHub and the AWS blog post Accelerate threat modeling with generative AI.
We welcome your feedback and questions in the comments.

articles.title: How Many Americans Are Millionaires?
paragraphs: If it feels like there are more millionaires in the U.S. than ever before, you’re right. According to the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, there are about 29 million U.S. households with a net worth (all assets minus all liabilities) exceeding $1 million. This represents roughly 22% of all U.S. households, a share which has more than doubled since 1998 (after adjusting for inflation):

However, most millionaires don’t have $1 million in their checking or brokerage accounts. The bulk of their wealth is tied up in their home equity and retirement accounts. If we excluded both, the number of millionaire households in the U.S. would drop by over 50%.

While this might seem obvious to some, it paints a complex picture of what it means to be a “millionaire” in America. This is why answering the question “How many Americans are millionaires?” technically depends on how you define one. Let’s dig in.

The classic definition of a millionaire is a $1M net worth. That is all of your assets (i.e., everything you own) minus all of your liabilities (i.e., everything you owe to others). While technically correct, some would argue that this definition is inaccurate because, for many, that wealth isn’t always easily accessible. After all, if you have a $1M home but only $10k in your checking account, do you really feel like a “millionaire”?
So let’s look at some additional definitions to classify millionaires:
With these definitions in mind, below is a summary of what share and total number of U.S. households fit into each (using the 2025 SCF data):
As you can see, while 21.5% of all U.S. households are millionaires based on the traditional definition, when we exclude illiquid assets, that percentage drops to just 6.1%.

This means that only around 28% of millionaires are millionaires based on their liquid net worth alone. You can see this in the chart below which shows the percentage of millionaires that fit into each definition:

If we excluded home equity and retirement accounts, not even half of millionaire households would still be considered millionaires. There’s nothing wrong with this, but it illustrates how much millionaire wealth is tied up in illiquid assets.
But regardless of how you define a millionaire, the share of U.S. households that fit each definition has gone up over time, especially in the last six years:
What’s interesting about this plot is how much housing has impacted millionaire wealth during certain time periods.

For example, from 2007 to 2010, the share of U.S. households that were millionaires (based on net worth) fell even as the share of millionaires (based on net worth excluding their home) rose. This illustrates how an inflated asset class (e.g., U.S. housing in 2007) can temporarily distort the number of millionaires we see in the data.
Now that we have looked at what a millionaire is, let’s turn to what millionaires own and why it varies by total wealth.

Before we can look at what millionaires own, we must first understand that not all millionaires are the same. After all, there’s a big difference between having $1M and having $10M. You can see it in the data too.

For example, there are nearly 10x more households with $1M-$10M than there are households with over $10M. You can see this in the plot below which shows the total number of millionaire households in the U.S. going back to 1989, based on inflation-adjusted net worth:
Though there are more decamillionaires today than ever before, it’s the absolute increase in millionaires ($1M+) over the last six years that has been the most profound.
When we break millionaire wealth down into smaller slices, we see that 77% of millionaires have less than $5M in net worth with the largest group (44%) having just $1M-$2M:
This illustrates the extreme right skew in millionaire wealth. In other words, the vast majority of millionaires are single-digit millionaires, not decamillionaires or centamillionaires.

This isn’t a problem, but it does change what these millionaires tend to own. If we were to look at the share of net worth allocated across various asset classes, we would see that the wealthier the millionaire, the more of their wealth sits in businesses and stocks (as opposed to home equity and retirement accounts):

For households with $1M-$2M, home equity makes up around 33% of their combined wealth, compared to just 7% for those with $10M+. Conversely, among those with $10M+, private businesses make up around 33% of their combined wealth, compared to 5% for those with $1M-$2M.

Of course, correlation doesn’t mean causation. You can start a business and buy all the stocks you want and there’s no guarantee that you’ll become a decamillionaire. Survivorship bias dominates the further we go up the wealth spectrum.
But it goes beyond that. Because most millionaires aren’t like most households. In fact, they tend to be atypical in one big way.

So far we’ve discussed millionaires as if they were a common occurrence in American society. And while they are less rare today than ever before, being one of them isn’t the norm, especially if you’re younger.
We can see this clearly if we look at the share of households within each age group that are millionaires:
As you can see, only 2% of households under 35 and 13% of households 35-44 have a $1M+ net worth. Compare this with households 55 and up, where over 30% are millionaires.
Putting it all together, the median age of U.S. millionaire households is 63. This means that half of all millionaire households are older than this.

So if you want to benchmark yourself against millionaires, you should make sure you’re around their age as well. If you’re not, then it’s not a fair comparison. After all, how can you equate yourself with people who’ve had an extra ten (or more) years to save and invest their money? That’s like comparing a kindergartner’s strength to a teenager’s.

And this goes beyond young people. Across America as a whole, millionaires are still in the minority. We can see this by looking at the number of households on the first four levels of The Wealth Ladder from 1989-2025:
While the share of U.S. households in Level 4 ($1M+) has increased in recent years, the vast majority of America (around 78%) still lives in Level 3 ($100k-$1M) or below.

While some on social media may claim that $1M is not a lot of money, it definitely is. This is true within America and even truer on a worldwide scale. According to UBS’s 2026 Global Wealth Report, having $1M in wealth would put you in the top 1.5% of adults globally. Even having just $100k would put you in the top 17%:
This demonstrates just how out of touch some people can be when it comes to having $1M (or more). Because being a millionaire in 2025 is still the exception, not the rule.
Of course, some of you won’t agree with me. Some of you won’t be swayed by global comparisons or by age adjustments. And that’s fine. But it doesn’t make them any less true.
I’m not here to convince you though. I just present the data and let you decide for yourself.

Because you can believe whatever you want. You can choose who to compare yourself with. You can compare yourself to the rich, or to the poor. To your most successful peers or to your least. Or to no one at all.
All I’m telling you is that being a millionaire, especially a young millionaire, is rare. What you make of that is up to you.
